title: St Nicholas Day in Poland: Mikołajki, Shoes and the Rózga
excerpt: St Nicholas Day in Poland is Mikołajki on 6 December: gifts in shoes and under pillows, the rózga, school gift draws and Gwiazdor.
metaDescription: St Nicholas Day in Poland is Mikołajki on 6 December: gifts in shoes and under pillows, the rózga, school gift draws and Gwiazdor.
summary: Mikołajki, St Nicholas Day, falls on 6 December: children find small gifts in a shoe, a sock or under the pillow after Mikołaj's night visit.
It is not a public holiday, so schools and offices hold a losowanie, a Secret Santa-style name draw with small gifts.
Naughty children are threatened with a rózga (twig), and on Christmas Eve some regions get gifts from Gwiazdor, Dzieciątko or Aniołek instead of Mikołaj.
The custom honours St Nicholas, a 4th-century bishop of Myra; the Masurian town of Mikołajki is named after a St Nicholas church, not the holiday.
featuredImageAlt: A pair of boots stuffed with small wrapped presents beside a bowl of nuts, the shoe-gift morning of St Nicholas Day in Poland on 6 December. Image by Hans from Pixabay
authorBio: PolishPal Contributor writes about Polish culture, history, and language for learners and the Polish diaspora.
factNotes: Origin of the word 'Mikołajki': the brief and keyword plan call it 'disputed', but no source I opened (Polish Wikipedia, powroty.gov.pl, several Polish news explainers) says so; the article says it found no reliable source for a dispute and describes it as derived from Mikołaj (the -ki pattern alongside Andrzejki/Walentynki is my own linguistic note, not sourced). Regional gift-bringers: sources conflict (Silesia is variously Dzieciątko, Aniołek or Józef; Małopolska is Aniołek or Gwiazdka), so the table is framed as a rough map; Gwiazdor = Wielkopolska (dzieje.pl, eska) plus Warmia (powroty.gov.pl); Gwiazdka = Lower Silesia (powroty) and southern Poland (eska). Left out: a claim that children polish their shoes beforehand (not found in Polish sources), Coca-Cola origin claims, and any specific gift price norms (the 50 zł limit appears only inside the fictional dialogue). The statement that a rózga today is mostly a joke/warning is a soft characterisation, not sourced. 'Wesołych Mikołajek' is presented as something you may see, not as a fixed formula. 6 Dec 2026 verified as a Sunday. Featured boots photo (Pixabay, Hans) is not claimed to be from Poland.
